title: SHE HID TWO MEN IN A WELL… THEN LOOKED THE KING’S SOLDIERS IN THE EYES
paragraphs: SHE HID TWO MEN IN A WELL… THEN LOOKED THE KING’S SOLDIERS IN THE EYES
The unnamed woman of 2 Samuel 17:17–21 who risked everything while David's kingdom was collapsing—and why her forgotten courage still speaks to every believer fighting battles nobody sees.
They were coming.

The king's men were searching for two messengers carrying information that could change the course of a rebellion. If those messengers were caught, David's enemies might gain the advantage they needed to destroy him.
And somewhere in Bahurim, inside an ordinary household, a woman was about to make a decision that would place her family in the path of a dangerous royal pursuit.
She wasn't a prophetess.
She wasn't a queen.
Scripture doesn't even tell us her name.
But when the messengers needed somewhere to disappear, she opened the door.
And when the pursuers arrived, she had already hidden the men in a well.
Think about that.
Some people are remembered because they stood before thousands.
Others are remembered by heaven because they refused to abandon someone when nobody was watching.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of this story is that the woman who helped protect David's messengers never received a recorded speech, a royal title, or even a name.
Yet her actions became part of the story of how God preserved David during one of the darkest betrayals of his life.
Before we talk about her courage, though, we need to understand why those two messengers were running.
Because behind that well was a broken father.
A rebellious son.
A divided kingdom.
And a king who was discovering that some of life's deepest wounds come from the people we love.
David was not fleeing a foreign invader.
He was fleeing Absalom.
His own son.
The same Absalom whose family had already been devastated by violence, whose anger had hardened into rebellion, and whose ambition had grown until he sought his father's throne.
David's household was suffering the consequences of years of sin, injustice, fractured relationships, and failures of leadership.
The Bible does not pretend David was innocent in everything that brought his family to this point.
This was the same David who had committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged Uriah's death.
The same David whom Nathan confronted with the terrible words:
"Thou art the man." — 2 Samuel 12:7, KJV
And now the consequences of sin had spread through his household in ways that no crown could conceal.
That is one reason this story matters.
God's grace does not require us to pretend that our past was harmless.
David had been forgiven, but forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
He was still God's anointed king, yet he was also a father carrying grief, regret, and the bitter fruit of choices he could not undo.
Maybe you understand that more than you wish you did.
Maybe you have repented of something, but the damage has taken longer to heal than you expected.
Maybe God has forgiven you, yet there are relationships still wounded by what happened.
Maybe you know what it feels like to pray for restoration while living with consequences.
David's story reminds us that God's mercy is real, even when life remains painfully complicated.
And in the middle of that complication, God used an unnamed woman.
Not someone with political authority.
Not someone commanding an army.
A woman with a household, a well, and a decision to make.
The biblical account begins with two men, Jonathan and Ahimaaz.
They were connected to the priests who remained in Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion. Their assignment was to carry urgent intelligence to David.
Hushai, David's loyal friend, had been working to frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel, whose military advice could have placed David in immediate danger.
The message was urgent: David needed to cross the Jordan rather than remain exposed in the wilderness.
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting near En-rogel because entering Jerusalem openly could expose them.
A female servant was to bring them the information.
Then they would carry it to David.
It was a fragile communication network, built on loyalty, secrecy, and the courage of people whose names history could easily overlook.
But someone saw them.
A young man reported their movements to Absalom.
And suddenly, the messengers were no longer simply carrying information.
They were being hunted.
Second Samuel 17:18 tells us:
"Nevertheless a lad saw them, and told Absalom: but they went both of them away quickly, and came to a man's house in Bahurim, which had a well in his court; whither they went down." — KJV
They came to a man's house.
There was a well in its courtyard.
And the two men climbed down into it.
Then the woman of the household stepped into the story.
"And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth, and spread ground corn thereon; and the thing was not known." — 2 Samuel 17:19, KJV
Read that again.
She covered the mouth of the well.
She spread grain over it.
She concealed the place where the messengers were hiding.
The Hebrew text gives this moment an extraordinary concreteness.

The word בְּאֵר (be'er) means a well or water source, and מָסָךְ (masakh) refers here to a covering. The grain described in the verse is רִפוֹת (rifot), generally understood as crushed or husked grain.
These are not mysterious religious symbols.
They are ordinary objects.
A well.
A covering.
Grain.
Household materials that became part of a life-preserving act.
And that is precisely what makes the scene so powerful.
She did not need a weapon to intervene.
She used what was already within her reach.
Sometimes faithfulness does not look dramatic from the outside.
Sometimes it looks like an ordinary person doing the necessary thing at the moment when doing nothing would be easier.
Then came the confrontation.
"And when Absalom's servants came to the woman to the house, they said, Where is Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" — 2 Samuel 17:20, KJV
Imagine the pressure of that question.
The men they were searching for were beneath the covering.
The hiding place was within the household.
One wrong movement could reveal everything.
Scripture does not tell us whether her hands trembled or whether her heart raced. It does not tell us who else was present, or exactly what the soldiers threatened.
We should not invent those details.
But the danger of the moment is unmistakable.
The pursuers had reached the very house where the messengers were concealed.
And the woman answered:
"They be gone over the brook of water." — 2 Samuel 17:20, KJV
The soldiers searched.
They did not find the messengers.
And they returned to Jerusalem.
Only after they had gone did the two men emerge.
"And it came to pass, after they were departed, that they came up out of the well, and went and told king David..." — 2 Samuel 17:21, KJV
The message reached David.
He was warned to cross the water quickly because of the counsel being given against him.
The following verse records that David and those with him crossed the Jordan before morning.
A crucial warning had arrived.
And the woman who hid the messengers had helped make that possible.
But here is where we must read carefully.
The Bible never says that the woman's entire household was saved from execution.
It does not record the soldiers threatening to kill her family, nor does it describe what happened to her household afterward.
What Scripture does show is that she sheltered the messengers, concealed their hiding place, and helped them escape discovery.
Her household became a refuge during a dangerous pursuit.
Her actions protected the messengers and contributed to the successful delivery of the warning to David.
That is already remarkable.
We do not need to add imaginary miracles to make God's Word powerful.
The truth is powerful enough.
And there is another difficult detail we cannot ignore.
The woman misdirected the pursuers.
She told them the messengers had gone elsewhere when, in fact, they were hidden in the well.
Does that mean Scripture is commanding believers to lie whenever they believe they have a good reason?
No.
The passage narrates her actions, but it does not explicitly pronounce every part of her conduct morally exemplary.
The wider biblical witness teaches that God is truthful and calls His people to truthfulness.
"Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour..." — Ephesians 4:25, KJV
At the same time, Scripture also records moments when people protected endangered lives from hostile authorities, including the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1 and Rahab in Joshua 2.
These accounts have prompted serious Christian reflection about truthfulness, protection of life, and moral responsibility under oppression.
We should neither erase the woman's courageous protection of the messengers nor pretend the ethical question does not exist.
Her story is not a blanket permission slip for dishonesty.
It is a historical account of an endangered mission, a woman who intervened, and a warning that reached the king.
And beneath all of it is a deeper lesson about the kind of people God uses.
People without titles.
People without platforms.
People whose names never appear in the spotlight.
People who do not have the luxury of waiting until courage feels comfortable.
Because courage is not always the absence of fear.
Sometimes courage is doing what is right while the outcome remains uncertain.
And there is something especially moving about the fact that the Bible preserves her actions without preserving her name.
We know what she did.
We know where she lived.
We know how she concealed the messengers.
But we do not know what people called her.
That should challenge something inside us.
We live in a world that measures importance by visibility.
How many people know your name?
How many people applaud your accomplishments?
How many people notice what you sacrifice?
But Scripture repeatedly reveals that God's purposes move through people the world would never consider important.
A servant girl carried information.
Two messengers carried a warning.
A woman opened her household.
A king crossed the Jordan.
And the rebellion did not end the way Absalom intended.
None of these human actions should be confused with the ultimate source of deliverance.
God remained sovereign over the outcome.
Yet His providence included the choices and actions of ordinary people.
That is a truth worth carrying into your own life.
Because you may be doing something right now that nobody appreciates.
You may be caring for an aging parent while others build careers.
You may be raising children while wondering whether your prayers are making any difference.
You may be quietly resisting temptation while nobody knows how close you came to surrendering.
You may be the only person in your household still opening the Bible.
The only one praying for reconciliation.
The only one refusing to return hatred for hatred.
And some days, you wonder whether any of it matters.
Listen carefully.
Your faithfulness does not become worthless simply because it is unseen.
Jesus said:
"Thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly." — Matthew 6:4, KJV
He was speaking specifically about giving without seeking public praise, but the principle reaches into our understanding of faithful obedience.
The Father sees what human applause cannot measure.
He sees the tears you wipe away before anyone enters the room.
He sees the prayers you cannot finish because your heart is exhausted.
He sees the temptation you resisted.
He sees the forgiveness you are struggling to extend.
He sees the acts of love that will never become public testimonies.
And He does not need a crowd to witness what He already knows.
But we must be careful not to turn this woman's story into a promise that every courageous decision will immediately rescue our families from suffering.
Some faithful believers suffer terribly.
Some courageous people are persecuted.
Some acts of obedience cost far more than we imagined.
Jesus never promised that following Him would remove every earthly danger.
He promised something greater than a painless life.
He promised His presence.
He promised eternal life to those who belong to Him.
He promised that death itself would not have the final word.
And this is where the story begins to point us toward a greater King.
David was an anointed king fleeing betrayal.
Jesus Christ, the Son of David, would also be betrayed.
But the resemblance has limits.
David was a sinner who needed forgiveness.
Jesus is the sinless Savior who gives forgiveness.
David fled to preserve his life during Absalom's rebellion.
Jesus willingly gave His life to save sinners.
David's messengers carried a warning that helped preserve a kingdom.
The apostles of Jesus would proclaim the Gospel announcing a Kingdom that cannot be shaken.
And where David's story exposes the brokenness of a royal household, the Gospel reveals the Son who obeyed His Father perfectly.
David could not heal the deepest corruption of the human heart.
Neither could a courageous woman in Bahurim.
Neither can you.
Neither can I.
But Jesus can redeem sinners, reconcile us to God, and begin transforming what sin has broken.
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, or gift.
In Ephesians 2, Paul presents salvation as God's gracious gift, received through faith, not as something we earn through our achievements.
That matters because some of us have spent years trying to prove that we are finally worthy of being loved by God.
We serve.
We sacrifice.
We give.
We work.
We hide our struggles.
And somewhere along the way, we begin to believe that if we do enough, perhaps God will finally accept us.
But the Gospel does not say that Jesus died to help you earn your salvation.
It says that Christ died for sinners.
That He was buried.
That He rose again.
And that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are found in Him.
Your obedience matters.
Your generosity matters.
Your service matters.
But none of those things purchases the blood of Christ.
Grace is not a reward for being impressive.
It is God's mercy toward people who could never rescue themselves.
And this is why our theme at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He declares every consequence irrelevant.
Not because every broken relationship is instantly restored.
But because sin and shame do not have to be the final authority over a life surrendered to Him.
The cross tells the truth about our sin.
The resurrection announces the victory of our Savior.
And the Gospel invites us to repent, believe, and walk in newness of life.
Maybe your story has a chapter you wish you could tear out.
Maybe there is something you did years ago that still visits your thoughts when the room becomes quiet.
Maybe you were betrayed by someone who should have protected you.
Maybe you were the one who caused the wound.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending that everything is fine.
Then hear this.
You do not need to manufacture a spotless past before coming to Jesus.
You need to come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in the Savior who died and rose again.
Receive His grace through faith.
And begin walking in the truth, even when healing takes time.
The unnamed woman in Bahurim could conceal two messengers beneath a covering.
But only Christ can deal with the sin we cannot cover ourselves.
David could cross the Jordan and escape an immediate threat.
But only Jesus can bring us through judgment into everlasting life.
And perhaps that is the most important difference in this entire story.
A hidden well could preserve a life for another day. The empty tomb announces life that death cannot conquer.
That is the hope we must never lose.
And that is why this account should change more than the way we remember an unnamed woman.
It should change the way we understand our own place in God's work.
You may never preach to a stadium.
You may never write a book.
You may never have thousands of followers.
But you can tell the truth about Jesus to someone who is searching.
You can open Scripture with a struggling friend.
You can pray for a person who feels abandoned.
You can help someone find a church where the Gospel is faithfully taught.
You can encourage a believer who is close to giving up.
You can become part of the quiet, faithful work through which others encounter the truth of Christ.
Not because you are their savior.
Because you know the Savior.
And perhaps someone in your life is waiting for a simple act of obedience from you.
A conversation you keep postponing.
An apology you have been too proud to offer.
A person you have been afraid to forgive.
A struggling believer you could encourage today.
Or a family member who needs to hear that Jesus still welcomes repentant sinners.
Do not underestimate what God can do through a life surrendered to Him.
But do not confuse faithfulness with fame.
The woman in Bahurim was not given a platform.
She was given a moment.
And she acted.
What will you do with yours?
If this story has exposed a hidden struggle, an unspoken fear, or a place where God is calling you to courage, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to disclose private details or prove your faith to strangers.
But sometimes a simple, sincere comment becomes the beginning of encouragement for someone else who thought they were suffering alone.
And if God has brought you through a season of shame, repentance, or restoration, share a little of that testimony if you feel comfortable.
Someone may need to hear that the grace of Jesus is not just something written on a page.
It is the hope that has kept you standing.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message.
Not because they are weak.
Not because they need to be publicly corrected.
But because they may be quietly asking whether their unseen faithfulness matters.

If Gospel-centered teaching like this has helped you, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those still exploring Christianity to follow as well.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, and genuine discipleship.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand that work, I want to speak plainly about something important.
Sharing the Gospel takes commitment.
Creating biblical teaching, developing discipleship materials, maintaining resources, and reaching more people require time, labor, and financial support.
At Gospel Warrior, we want to continue making Christian learning resources accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
Those resources are part of our desire to serve, not merely to build an audience.

Some believers choose to set aside a regular portion of their giving for Gospel-centered ministries. If you are prayerfully considering that kind of support, Gospel Warrior is one ministry you may choose to include.
But I want to be biblically clear.
Supporting your local church, caring for those in need, and practicing faithful stewardship remain important Christian responsibilities.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek expression μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs) means not out of grief or reluctance, and not out of compulsion.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not the fear that God will love you less if you cannot afford to give.
But voluntary generosity flowing from gratitude to Christ and a sincere desire to help others hear His Word.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities for meaningful conversations about faith.
It is the opportunity to participate in work intended to point people toward Christ.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read.
You can still learn.
You can still pray with us.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
Because Gospel ministry should never become a place where people are made to feel that grace has a price tag.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
We are simply seeking to make His truth known.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me one final time to that house in Bahurim.
The messengers are hidden.
The well is covered.
The pursuers have come and gone.
The woman has done what she could.
And when the danger passes, the men emerge and continue their mission.
They carry the warning to David.
The king and his people cross the Jordan.
And the woman disappears from the narrative.
No recorded celebration.
No recorded reward.
No final description of her life.
Just an extraordinary moment of courage preserved in the Word of God.
Thousands of years later, we are still reading about what she did.
And that should make us wonder.
How many faithful acts are happening today that will never be noticed by the world?
How many parents are praying through the night?
How many believers are quietly refusing to compromise?
How many people are opening their homes, sharing their food, offering encouragement, or standing beside someone who has nowhere else to turn?
How many ordinary Christians are serving Christ without ever knowing how their obedience may affect another life?
You may not see the full fruit of your faithfulness.
The woman in Bahurim did not know everything that would happen after the messengers left her house.
And neither do we.
But we know the One who holds history in His hands.
We know the Son of David who came not merely to preserve an earthly throne, but to redeem sinners.
We know the Savior who was rejected, crucified, buried, and raised in glory.
And because Jesus lives, no life surrendered to Him is without hope.
So stop measuring your spiritual significance by how many people applaud you.
Stop assuming that your ordinary life cannot be useful in the hands of an extraordinary God.
Stop allowing the shame of yesterday to silence the obedience He is calling you to today.
Repent where you need to repent.
Seek forgiveness where you have done wrong.
Trust Christ where fear has taken hold.
And be faithful with what He has placed before you.
Maybe all you have is a small opportunity.
A quiet conversation.
A difficult act of kindness.
A Bible opened across a kitchen table.
A prayer spoken through tears.
A door opened to someone who needs help.
The woman in Bahurim had a well, a covering, and a moment in which to act.
And God preserved her story in Scripture.
But remember this above everything else:
Our hope is not ultimately in being as brave as that woman.
Our hope is in Jesus Christ, who was faithful where we have failed, who died for our sins, and who rose again so that all who trust in Him may have life.
Above all, let this story lead you past admiration for an unnamed woman and into deeper trust in the Savior whose grace is sufficient.
Because when the world forgets your name, when the people you helped never thank you, and when the doors close without applause, there is still One who sees.
The world may never know the name of the person who held the door open—but someone may reach safety because they did.
